input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane in the form of vapour. In this study, a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane are compared using the same feed, and the comparison is notable in that it reports flux, separation factor and stability together, three characteristics that are seldom reported together for the same membrane. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m⁻² h⁻¹), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. The feed used in the tests consisted of 85 wt% ethanol in water, at a temperature of 60 °C. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 1.8 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ together with a separation factor of 180; however, its flux fell by 14% over the course of 500 h. In contrast, the zeolite membrane achieved a flux of 1.1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a separation factor of 320, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Overall, the two membranes exhibit a clear trade-off between flux on the one hand and separation performance and stability on the other. The polymer membrane allows more mass to pass per unit area, so that a given duty at its flux would require less membrane area, but it separates less sharply and progressively loses flux as the test proceeds. The zeolite membrane, by comparison, allows less mass to pass but separates more sharply and maintains its flux over the duration tested, meaning that the permeate it produces stands further from the feed composition, albeit at the cost of more area for the same throughput. It should be noted that only one feed composition was tested, and that no test was run beyond 500 h; consequently, the comparison is valid at that composition and within that duration, and the behaviour of the membranes at other feed compositions, together with their stability over longer periods of service, remains outside the scope of these tests.
